title: Test one change, prove the result, plan 90 days

say: Test one change, prove the result, and plan your next 90 days.
This is the video for Module 4 of Productivity and Time Management at Work.
Saying I am very organised is a claim. Showing that you cut interruptions from 23 to 7 a day is evidence. Employers, clients and partners trust evidence.

panel.rule: One change only, so you can tell whether it worked

say: Rukayat's baseline showed 6 meetings a day, spread from 9 to 4. Her hypothesis: if I move meetings to 1 to 4, and block 9 to 11:30 for deep work, my focused hours will rise to at least 2 a day.
In week 1, two client meetings still land in the morning, so she offers afternoon slots. Over two weeks, focused hours average 1.9 a day.

card.title: Rukayat tests meeting blocks
rows: Focused hours a day, two weeks

say: Her weekly priorities rise from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5. She keeps the change, and adjusts it to allow client mornings once a week.
And if your numbers do not improve, that is still evidence. Write why, and what you would adjust.

say: Then value. Managers think in results and money. If each extra sales visit brings one order in four, and an order earns about 10000 naira profit, 4 extra visits a week is roughly one extra order. Always label estimates as estimates.

say: A claim with no numbers is easy to ignore.

Bukola, the Lagos caterer, writes a CV line instead. She redesigned customer messaging with WhatsApp Business quick replies, reducing daily interruptions by about 80 percent while keeping same-day replies.
In interviews, use STAR: the situation, the task, the action you took, and the result with numbers. Practise it in under two minutes.

Report your real numbers, including what did not improve. Leave colleagues' names and client details out of anything you share outside your organisation, and ask your manager before posting work data publicly.

No colleague names or client details

say: 90 days matches a business quarter, the same period as an OKR. Score your Module 1 OKR from 0 to 1 for each key result, then write a sharper new one.
Name your next biggest time drain and the change you will test.
Put your daily plan, deep-work block, message batches, shutdown routine and weekly review into Google Calendar as repeating events, not intentions.
And plan for slips. If I miss my weekly review two weeks in a row, I will do a 20-minute version on Monday morning.

say: To remember. Test one change against your baseline, with a hypothesis written first. Show evidence, not claims, and label estimates. Schedule your keeper habits, and decide now how you will restart when they slip.
